strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem of discovering instance-specific symmetries from unlabeled data
Mathematically principled framework with convergence guarantees via Fréchet mean normalization
Effective handling of partial symmetries, demonstrated by distinguishing between different rotation subgroups on MNIST
Comprehensive experimental implementation details enabling reproducibility, with promised code release
Demonstrates multi-domain evaluation spanning 2D imaging and 3D molecular conformations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution (Fréchet mean for canonical normalization) is an incremental application of standard differential geometry concepts rather than a conceptual breakthrough

Weak theoretical justification: Proposition 3.1 only guarantees asymptotic convergence; practical implications for finite samples are unclear, and why Fréchet mean is the right choice over other Lie group centrality measures is not rigorously justified

Narrow experimental scope: 2D experiments limited to simple digit datasets with obvious symmetries; 3D experiments focus almost exclusively on SO(3) rotations, while other groups mentioned in introduction are not thoroughly evaluated
Insufficient baseline comparisons: limited empirical comparison with recent methods beyond SGM and IE-AE; many related works mentioned but not empirically compared against
Unclear validation of correctness: for unlabeled data, there is no ground truth to verify recovered symmetry distributions are actually correct; validation relies largely on visual inspection

Methodological concerns: the k-NN approximation of classes [x] introduces errors with unclear propagation; sensitivity to threshold ε in Eq. (1) is not analyzed; simplified noise model lacks robustness analysis
Limited discussion of failure cases: Section 6 is brief; method's assumptions (compact Lie groups, class-decomposability) limit applicability with insufficient analysis of when it fails
Weak practical motivation: unclear when practitioners should prefer RECON over simpler alternatives; out-of-distribution detection application feels somewhat disconnected from the main narrative
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices: k=25 for k-NN and other design decisions lack thorough justification or ablation studies
Dense presentation: heavy mathematical notation and lack of clear intuitive explanation for why Fréchet mean solves the arbitrary canonicalization problem

strengths: Novel canonical orientation normalization technique that elegantly solves the arbitrary pose problem in class-pose decomposition with strong theoretical justification via Proposition 3.1
Strong theoretical foundation with rigorous mathematical grounding in group theory and Fréchet means, including formal proofs of convergence in Wasserstein distance
Comprehensive experimental validation on both synthetic (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST) and real-world data (molecular conformations), successfully recovering complex symmetries including SO(2) and SO(3)
Clear demonstration of interpretability advantages over existing methods, with data-aligned canonical poses (e.g., upright digits) versus arbitrary orientations
Practical applications demonstrated (OOD pose detection with AUC 0.92-0.80, molecular conformation analysis) showing real-world relevance beyond toy problems
Excellent reproducibility with publicly available code, detailed implementation details in appendices, and comprehensive experimental setup descriptions
Ability to handle challenging cases including partial symmetries (e.g., distinguishing 6's from 9's related by 180° but not full SO(2) equivalence)
weaknesses: Limited scope of demonstrated symmetries restricted primarily to rotation groups (SO(2), SO(3)); framework claims generality to arbitrary Lie groups but lacks validation on reflection symmetries or discrete groups
Incomplete experimental comparisons with only SGM and IE-AE as direct baselines; missing quantitative comparisons with other recent symmetry discovery methods mentioned in related work
Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: choice of k=25 neighbors appears arbitrary with no systematic method provided, and only limited sensitivity analysis shown
MNIST/Fashion-MNIST evaluation uses artificially labeled data with known ground-truth symmetries, validating recovery but not fully testing discovery from truly unknown distributions
Molecular conformations evaluation focuses on reconstruction quality rather than validating discovered symmetries, lacking quantitative ground truth and comparison with structure-based methods
Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic discussion of failure cases, robustness to noise/corruption, computational complexity limitations, or edge cases with complex partial symmetries

Presentation clarity issues: dense mathematical notation could be simplified, connection between canonical orientation normalization and symmetric discovery could be more intuitive, some key details relegated to appendix
Limited statistical rigor: some results lack error bars or significance testing, single runs shown without confidence intervals, and limited discussion of variance across different initializations

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly articulates the limitation of arbitrary canonicals in class-pose methods with effective illustrations
Theoretically grounded solution: Proposition 3.1 provides solid mathematical foundation using Fréchet means on Lie groups with detailed convergence proof
Architecture-agnostic and practical: method works without retraining as a drop-in solution, enabling test-time canonicalization of pre-trained models
Comprehensive experimental validation: tests on both 2D (MNIST, FashionMNIST) and 3D (GEOM-QM9) data with first extension to 3D symmetry discovery
Strong downstream applications: substantial test-time canonicalization improvements (92.94% vs 66.90% on MNIST) and effective OOD detection
Thorough ablations and analysis: neighborhood size effects, equivalence class quality validation (0.95 hit rate), partial symmetry handling, data efficiency
Elegant and simple core idea: right-multiplication by inverse Fréchet mean is intuitive, implementable, and geometrically principled
Excellent presentation: well-written with clear motivation (Figure 1), consistent notation, and extensive reproducibility details
Thoughtful extensions: Tukey-Fréchet mean handles multimodal distributions robustly (Appendix C)
weaknesses: Fundamental scope limitation: complete dependency on class-pose decompositions limits applicability; fails when group action is on entire input rather than objects (acknowledged limitation for natural images)
Vulnerability to backbone quality: RECON entirely inherits IE-AE limitations with no robustness analysis or fallback mechanisms; k-NN approximation fails with poorly-separated classes
Substantial performance gaps on downstream tasks: GEOM 55.70% vs 97.01% perfect canonicalization (41.3% gap) raises practical deployment concerns; gaps of 5-10% on image tasks also significant

Limited baseline comparisons: primarily compares against IE-AE backbone itself; SGM (most relevant work) only compared qualitatively on one metric without quantitative comparison on symmetry discovery accuracy

Theoretical assumptions insufficiently validated: noise model (Eq. 1) assumes group transformations + small noise but never empirically validated; ε′ bound never quantified; what happens with structural variations?

Incomplete 3D evaluation: only synthetic rotations on GEOM, no naturally-occurring symmetries; 80% success rate with high variance; no comparison with other 3D symmetry methods; high errors (Figure 6c) unexplained

Insufficient failure analysis: GEOM molecules with high error unexplained despite Figure 12 analysis; no characterization of which symmetry distributions work better/worse; single-run results without confidence intervals
Ad-hoc equivalence class definition: theoretical definition (connected proximity) not used in practice; k=25 chosen empirically not principally; hit rate noise accumulation not addressed
Restrictive parametric form assumption: Section 3.3 limits to known parametric families; complex distributions require non-parametric alternatives (flow models) mentioned but not implemented
Missing computational analysis: no computational costs, timing comparisons, or Fréchet mean complexity discussion; practical scalability unclear
Incremental technical novelty: Fréchet means are standard, learnable mappings Θ and Λ are simple MLPs; main novelty is problem formulation and application rather than new methods
Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-seed reporting; single-run experiments make reproducibility assessment difficult

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly articulates the arbitrary canonical orientation problem in class-pose methods with effective visual illustration
Principled mathematical framework: Proposition 3.1 formally justifies Fréchet mean normalization using rigorous Wasserstein distance convergence arguments
Extension to 3D and realistic molecular data: validates on SO(3) and large-scale GEOM-QM9 dataset, extending beyond prior 2D-only symmetry discovery work
Multiple practical applications: demonstrates OOD detection and test-time canonicalization without architectural changes or retraining
Ability to capture partial symmetries: correctly distinguishes between related classes (digits 6 vs 9) where full equivariance methods fail
Comprehensive experimental documentation: detailed appendices with implementation details and hyperparameter choices support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is a straightforward post-processing step (right-multiply by empirical Fréchet mean), providing incremental rather than fundamental methodological advances

Severely restricted applicability: fundamentally limited to scenarios where group action operates on entire inputs; fails for natural images with objects in cluttered backgrounds, as acknowledged but minimized in Section 6
Weak empirical validation on realistic data: MNIST/FashionMNIST use synthetic uniform rotations; GEOM uses synthetic matrix-Fisher rotations; no validation on naturally occurring symmetries

Unexplained failure modes: ~20% of GEOM molecules show high prediction error (MSE > 800) with authors claiming 'no clear correlation' to molecular properties, suggesting possible spurious pattern learning
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compares to IE-AE and SGM; missing comparisons to VPGCNN, Partial G-CNNs, Augerino, and frame averaging despite citing them
Theory-practice gap: Proposition 3.1 assumes neural network continuity and small noise, but lacks finite-sample complexity analysis, convergence rates, or empirical validation of assumptions
Equivalence class definition issues: formal ε-connected component definition is impractical; k-NN approximation quality unanalyzed; Figure 10 shows 23.2% of molecules with hit rate < 0.9
Suspicious result magnitudes: test-time canonicalization gap (92.94% vs 14.69% on MNIST) raises fairness concerns; results seem unusually favorable to RECON
Learned mappings propagate errors: Θ and Λ trained on pseudo-labels from Algorithm 1 without principled error analysis; no ablation removing this stage
Missing key ablations and analyses: no comparison to simpler alternatives (median pose), no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters beyond k, no zero-shot transfer analysis

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying concrete limitation (arbitrary canonicals in class-pose methods) with well-motivated solution
Solid theoretical contribution with Proposition 3.1 providing convergence guarantees in Wasserstein distance and rigorous proofs
Comprehensive experimental validation spanning 2D (MNIST, FashionMNIST) and 3D (GEOM-QM9) with first SO(3) symmetry discovery demonstrations
Practical value: architecture-agnostic test-time canonicalization without retraining shows significant improvements (92.94% vs 66.90% on Rot-MNIST)
Thoughtful handling of multimodal distributions via Tukey-Fréchet mean extension with clear motivation and convergence analysis
Ability to distinguish classes related by group transformations (digits 6 and 9), which full equivariance methods cannot achieve
Extensive ablation studies, implementation details, and reproducibility artifacts (promised code release, hyperparameter documentation)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution (right-multiplication by inverse Fréchet mean) uses standard statistical tools (Fréchet means, M-estimators) without significant methodological innovation
Fundamental dependence on class-pose decomposition methods (IE-AEs), which are niche architectures, limiting practical applicability and scope of impact
Equivalence class definition via k-NN proximity in invariant space Z is heuristic and lacks theoretical justification; assumes well-separated clusters that may not exist
Weak baseline comparisons: SGM (closest related work) compared only qualitatively; missing quantitative symmetry recovery accuracy comparisons
Limited real-world evaluation: image experiments only on synthetic rotations of MNIST/FashionMNIST; no natural image experiments where acknowledged background/object context challenges arise
Approximately 20% of molecules show high prediction error (MSE > 800) on GEOM-QM9 (Figure 5d); root causes not identified beyond ruling out molecular size/flexibility correlation
Theoretical assumptions restrictive: assumes s = ρ_X(g)γ[x] + ε_s with ||ε_s|| < ε' (small noise) and well-defined classes; realistic validity on diverse data unclear
No computational complexity analysis; scalability of k-NN searches and Fréchet mean computations to large-scale datasets not discussed
